title: Just give them a calculator
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton uses a Year 10 bottom-set lesson on adding fractions to challenge the view that weaker students simply cannot retain procedures. Sitting beside one student, he saw that finding multiples and multiplying numerators consumed so much of her attention that she lost the procedure's steps. Citing Willingham's idea that memory is the residue of thought, he hypothesises that arithmetic is diverting thought from the procedure. He recommends keeping numbers simple and letting students use calculators freely, checking each step on mini-whiteboards. He rejects the objection that non-calculator exams demand non-calculator practice, and adds that low attainers are often least proficient with calculators and need practice.
points: Students who repeatedly forget procedures may be failing to think about the steps because arithmetic absorbs their attention, not because of a memory deficit.
Using simple numbers such as 2s, 5s and 10s keeps attention on the procedure until its steps are automated.
Letting students use calculators offloads arithmetic so they can think hard about the order and reasons for each step.
Calculator use must be guarded by step-by-step checks on mini-whiteboards and full working out, so students do not just type in the answer.
Even top sets should use calculators to check answers, which builds proficiency and speeds up feedback.
quotes: Students are taught key procedures repeatedly, yet, to everyone’s frustration - because, believe me, the students feel this as acutely as we do - it does not stick.
Not only did this take time, it also sapped her attention. Hence, when she finished her list, she couldn't recall the next step: finding the lowest number that appears in both lists.

I hypothesise that the issue is not some inability of a certain type of student to retain information. It is because students’ attention has been diverted away from what they need to be thinking about - the steps of the procedures - because so much attention needs to be expended on the arithmetic.
First, keep the numbers as simple as possible. 2s, 5s and 10s are usually safe bets.

Instead, if we allow students to use their calculator whenever they like - and openly encourage it - students offload the burden of doing the arithmetic. They can dedicate more of their attention to the steps of the procedures - both the order and why they are doing them.

Students who most need a calculator are often the least proficient in using one. Anyone who has marked calculator papers at GCSE will see low-achieving students use written methods for multiplications that they could just put in their calculator.

When students learn a new idea, we want as much of their attention to be on that idea as possible. If a lack of arithmetic skills will divert their attention away from thinking hard about the idea, offload that attention by giving them a calculator.
